articles.title: EDA: Observe, Verify, and Assess for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Depression Analysis
articles.summary: Existing multimodal depression assessment methods often summarize long recordings into global behavioral descriptions. This leaves the source and decision relevance of individual observations difficult to inspect. We propose EDA, an evidence-grounded framework organized around Observe, Verify, and Assess. In Observe, literature-informed acoustic and visual cues are localized into source-linked Evidence Records with temporal intervals and behavioral measurements. In Verify, frozen multimodal agents examine whether the cited media support each observation. The simplified Support admission policy retains positively verified records and their review grounds. In Assess, statistical descriptors and temporal events support reference-based behavioral comparison, while PHQ-9-guided text analysis provides complementary symptom evidence. Cross-modal disagreement triggers review of the original text before final selection. Experiments on D-Vlog and LMVD evaluate human-referenced cue agreement and downstream assessment utility separately. AI cue annotations achieve 91.02% accuracy against human consensus labels on shared source segments. With a frozen 7B backbone, EDA Support improves F1 over direct prediction by 7.61 and 9.88 percentage points on D-Vlog Leave-Query-Out and LMVD, respectively. These findings support explicit, source-linked behavioral evidence for inspectable multimodal depression assessment.

articles.title: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction
articles.summary: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, but in sequential deployment, standard coverage guarantees can still allow substantial fluctuations in the number of miscoverages over time. We study an online setting in which prediction sets are produced one round at a time and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a prescribed budget throughout deployment.Such a hard coverage guarantee can be enforced by enlarging prediction sets, but how much additional prediction-set size is fundamentally necessary remains unclear. We characterize this unavoidable efficiency cost over $T$ prediction rounds. Remarkably, the cost persists even with i.i.d.\ data, a known score distribution, and perfect knowledge of the population-optimal prediction set. Under suitable regularity conditions relating coverage and prediction-set size, we determine the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size required by any online method satisfying the hard coverage constraint. This minimum cost is $Θ(\log T)$ for expected cost at a fixed time known in advance, $Θ(T^{1/3})$ for the largest expected cost over all fixed times up to $T$, and $Θ(\sqrt{T})$ for the expected worst realized cost when the evaluation time is chosen in hindsight. We further show that these rates can be attained using past scores, without knowing the score distribution. Thus, even perfect statistical knowledge does not make sequential reliability free.

articles.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
articles.summary: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. articles.summary: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. articles.title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
articles.summary: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories. Three experiments are conducted: exploratory analysis with three input features, scalability analysis with increasing dimensionality (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a selected representative configuration. Across all scenarios, both classical and quantum approaches captured the relationship between the inputs and the main-engine fuel-flow rate, maintaining strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R2 (0.991 in the performance comparison conducted with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features, for instance) and the lowest aggregate imputation errors, while the radial basis function kernel was the strongest classical baseline, delivering highly competitive results.

articles.title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
articles.summary: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.

articles.title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
articles.summary: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

articles.title: What is the best harness for each model?
articles.content:
TL;DR
We partnered with
Baseten
to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions:
when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model?
Previously, our
v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard
ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3.
V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses Ã 5 models Ã 62 tasks Ã 4 attempts, 76Ã the size of v1.0.
Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience.
Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3.
Cost ranks moved far between models.
By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3.
Result
Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness
Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post.
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%.
Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points).
Why We Built
FrontierHarness
Eval v1.1
V1.0
ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another.
V1.1 runs each harness with five models.
What We Tested
Harnesses.
18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the
appendix
gives their versions.
Models.
Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 (
zai-org/GLM-5.3
), GLM Flash (
zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash
), DeepSeek (
deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017
), Muse (
meta-models/muse-spark-open
) and Kimi-K3 (
moonshotai/Kimi-K3
).
Tasks.
62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours.
Setup and Scoring
Configuration and Runtime
We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harnessâs default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort.
Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial
Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial.
Scoring Method
Table 1. Methodology
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of
our dashboard
:
Average cost per task:
the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5).
Cost per pass:
the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7).
We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate Ã· cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line.
Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model.
Results by Model
Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63.
How Sure Are These Results?
We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%).
The Harness Changes the Cost
The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts:
Model, 92.8%:
the differences between the five models.
Harness, 2.3%:
the part of the effect of a harness that is the same with every model.
Pair, 4.9%:
the rest. It also contains noise, because each cell has one value.
So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise.
With the Model Fixed, the Harness Changes the Cost by 1.8 to 5.0 Times
Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model
Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest.
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. âChanceâ is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one.
The Cheapest Harness per Task Changes With the Model
Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task)
Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3.
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse.
Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26.
A Higher Cost Does Not Give a Higher Score
Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model
This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from â0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often.
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one.
Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less?
No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass.
Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are.
Start tokens:
the input tokens of the first agent-loop request: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the task.
Tools:
the tools that the first request offers.
Cache hit rate and steps:
the mean over the passed trials. A step is one entry of the agent trajectory.
Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was â0.03 to +0.02 (p â¥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the
appendix
give the values.
Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass.
Table 4. Start tokens, tools, cache hit rate, steps and cost per pass of each harness
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
Where the Cost Comes From
Figure 8. Inference cost of each harness, by token type or by trial outcome
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
All costs are inference estimates at list prices. The pass rate of the harness on the model card has an outline.
Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%.
Tokens and the Cache
The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9).
Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens)
This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
One pair shows the effect of the cache.
Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task)
read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost.
Most of the Cost Goes to Trials That Do Not Pass
64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass
: 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts.
What the Best-Value Harnesses Share
The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests.
One shell tool does most of the work.
By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Piâs
default prompt
has four tools and sends file searches to
bash
:
selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])],
addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find");
Each request only adds to the one before it.
The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens:
# Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd)
request  prompt tokens  cached tokens
   8        15,954         15,616
   9        16,351         15,936
  10        16,999         16,320
No subagents and almost no summaries.
Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6):
.map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10);
The five also share a weakness.
Failed runs end with a confident answer.
About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete:
# Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e)
Agent:    - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and
            cancellation-cleanup tests.
Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent
          assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2
          AssertionError: a

articles.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
articles.content:
Engineering
How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
AUTHOR
Addy Osmani
CATEGORY
Engineering
PUBLISHED
Nov 16, 2026
READING TIME
10
min
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and
reviewed by Claude
. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.
Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.
Thatâs because giving agents a
way to verify their output
is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claudeâs work against a rubric
improved task success by up to 10 points
over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.
What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.
You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agentâs performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.
So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.
NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN
No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.
If your tests are flaky youâll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before youâve committed the changes.
Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.
E2E tests
If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.
The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to foolâeither the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you whatâs broken.
FIG A
A unit test may show âError: Timeout after 30 seconds,â but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of whatâs broken.
While unit tests are faster and less flaky, itâs possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test donât understand the full task.
With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like
CDP
, simulators, or API harnesses.
The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the userâs point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.
Property tests: constraints that canât break
A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.
You start by writing a statement you think canât fail and then use a test library (
fast-check
for JS/TS,
Hypothesis
for Python,
proptest
for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.
There are many properties in virtually every software project like:
Round-trip encoding
: âif you encode X then decode it back, you get X.â This works for parsing and serialization as well.
Invariants
: Things that must always be true, like âaccount balance can never become negative.â
Idempotency
: Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once.
Equivalence
: Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code.
Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that arenât created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.
Differential tests: the old system is the oracle
Differential tests are particularly effective for
large-scale migration
use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.
The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. Youâll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.
HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION
We have previously written about
how code review works at Anthropic
, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.
Verification means running the change
Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.
Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.
To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.
Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.
When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.
Failing tests require human attention
Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.
Code owners write their own checks
The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.
Reliability checks trigger on the diff
We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is â--resume loads old transcripts.â When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts wonât have it.
Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matchesâusually 3 to 10âso nobody has to memorize past outages.
One reviewer, multiple rounds
We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a
REVIEW.md
that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.
We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. Itâs cheaper and finds more.
Changes can't modify their own checks
If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch,
never from the pull request's changes
. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.
The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.
The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a
hook
that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a
/goal
of a passing test suite.
Start a new gate in observe mode
In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.
We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.
Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.
Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck â Claude Code isn't perfect.
Test your checks on what actually matters
The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.
This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our
code review post
, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.
They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.
In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.
Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as
Important, Nit or Pre-existing
. The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.
Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.
Turn misses into rules

articles.title: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
articles.content:
Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to websites by 40%
November 9, 2026
Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic.
Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking
  brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the
  practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present
  on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little
  evidence for any other tactic.
Google answers first
An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew
  on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in
  September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the
  featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the
  discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is
  down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset
  covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches.
  Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900
  US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for
  those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's.
You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third
  quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent:
Search intent
Q4 2025
Q3 2026
Informational (looking something up)
48.42%
70.44%
Commercial (comparing options)
26.30%
51.35%
Navigational (looking for a site)
17.04%
34.03%
Transactional (ready to buy)
10.82%
28.64%
Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026,
  keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. 
  A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers
  difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing
  advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51
  and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time. 
  The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining
  at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%.
Queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. Over a year, queries of five or more words grew from 29.3% to
  34.8% of unique desktop queries and from 29.6% to 31.9% on mobile. Three and four word searches are still the most
  common.
What happens to the clicks
The strongest evidence is an experiment. Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen gave US desktop Chrome users an extension that
  put each of them at random into a group. One group saw Google as usual, and another had AI Overviews hidden. The
  researchers then watched two weeks of real searches in January and February 2026. On searches that would show an Overview, the group that could see them averaged 0.37 clicks
  to outside websites per search, against 0.62 for the group that couldn't, which the authors report as a 39.8% reduction.
  Searches ending with no outbound click went from 54% to 73%. Clicks on ads didn't change, which suggests Google takes
  care not to cannibalize its own revenue. Across all searches, with and without an Overview, the authors put the loss
  at roughly 18.5% of the organic clicks a site gets from Google. The authors expect the loss to grow as Overviews appear on more
  searches. This is a randomized controlled trial, the most reliable kind of study for separating cause
  from correlation or coincidence. The effect was statistically significant for informational searches.
  The navigational and transactional samples were too small to settle anything. 
  This is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop only. A separate preregistered experiment by Wang and colleagues, with 1,100
  people, also found that removing AI Overviews and AI Mode raised clicks to publishers.
Observational data points the same way. Pew found people clicked an ordinary result on 8% of visits to a results page
  with a summary and on 15% without one, and ended their browsing session on 26% against 16%. Pew's comparison isn't a
  controlled experiment, because the searches that draw a summary tend to be longer and phrased as questions.
Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of people shown a result who click it. Across more
  than 2,000 websites in DataForSEO's panel, the desktop CTR of the first organic result fell from 17.83% in September
  2025 to 7.43% in August 2026, a drop of 58%. Mobile fell from 25.17% to 20.80%, a drop of 17%.
Desktop lost nearly half its click-through rate in one month, March 2026, and stayed down. Mobile fell about as far
    over five months, then recovered most of it. These figures come from Table A2 of the report.
Desktop plunged from 15.18% to 7.94% between February and March 2026. AI Overviews can't easily explain that step
  since the report has them almost flat that month, at 42.79% and then 43.38%. A change in the format or quality of the
  Overviews might explain part of it, though that is speculation on our part.
  Mobile, meanwhile, sank to 12.96% and then rebounded to 22.49% by
  May. The report itself says its data "does not establish" whether AI answers, layout changes, or changes in behavior
  are the cause. Its sample may also be shifting underneath it, since the unique desktop queries it counts fell by a
  third over the year, from 1.97 million to 1.32 million. Whatever the cause, a top ranking on desktop now earns less
  than half the clicks it did a year earlier.
DataForSEO also estimates where clicks go on pages with and without an Overview. By its model, the first organic result
  holds 9 to 16 points less click share on pages with one, though these are different searches on a single day's snapshot:
Search intent
Position 1, no Overview
Position 1, with Overview

The click share for the Overview's cited links looks promising, but it comes from a model. Pew, which logged real
  browsing, saw people click a link inside a summary on just 1% of visits, against 8% for ordinary results. Eighteen months and a large change in the product
  separate the two measurements, so it is difficult to say which is closer to the truth.
Google disputes that search traffic to websites is declining. In August 2025 its head of Search, Liz Reid, wrote that total organic clicks were
  "relatively stable year-over-year" and that Google was sending "slightly more quality clicks", meaning clicks where
  people don't quickly come back. She gave no figures to back that up.
Your site can't see whether someone goes back to Google, so you can't check Google's quality-clicks claim yourself, but
  you can check what your Google clicks are worth.
RevScope
, our product, shows your revenue per visitor
  from Google, AI Overviews included, and which landing pages earn the most.
Who the answers cite
If people read the summary and stop there, it matters which sites the summary cites. The report compares Google's AI
  Overviews with ChatGPT. Their most-cited lists overlap, but a different kind of site leads each one.
Rank

The report warns that the two platforms' counts aren't comparable, so compare where a site ranks within each list. Reddit and
  Wikipedia rank near the top of both, and by our count 16 of the 30 domains in each top 30 appear on both lists. The
  differences are still large. YouTube is first in AI Overviews and nineteenth in ChatGPT. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok
  make Google's top ten and miss ChatGPT's top 30, while Reuters, The Guardian, AP News, and The Washington Post make
  ChatGPT's top 30 and miss Google's. ChatGPT also often cites nobody: 27.3% of its answers had no source, against 0.7% for
  AI Overviews. So, as the report puts it, strength on one platform "doesn't automatically guarantee" the same on another.
Reddit also appears in Google's ordinary top ten for 32.15% of the report's tracked results, nearly eight times Quora's
  4.11%. Two limits apply to all of this. The first is that the answers come from prompts DataForSEO collected, and the report
  doesn't explain how they were chosen or whether they match what people really ask. The second is that big platforms do
  about as well in ordinary results: Pew found Wikipedia, YouTube, and Reddit made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries
  and 17% of those in standard results. Still, the common belief that AI favors Reddit holds up in this data.
GEO looks mostly like SEO
Google's position is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI
  Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary", beyond a page being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Since
  that is a company describing its own product, we looked at outside data on two questions. The first is 
  which sites get considered, and the second is which page on a site gets picked.
Which sites: link profiles correlate with citations
A referring domain is another website that links to yours. DataForSEO measured
  how closely referring domains track AI citations using Spearman's correlation, a score where 0 means no relationship
  between two rankings and 1 means they match exactly. The score was 0.406 for AI Overviews and 0.377 for ChatGPT. Links
  marked as coming from user-generated content, such as forum posts, scored lower, at 0.342 and 0.314.
These are moderate relationships, and they don't show that links cause citations, since large, well-known sites tend
  to have more of everything. The samples also contain only domains cited at least once, so they can't tell you what it
  takes to get cited for the first time. A similar pattern shows up in ordinary rankings: domains ranking first had a
  median of 111 referring domains against 85 for positions 4 to 10, with heavy overlap between the groups. For AI
  Overviews, the median cited domain had 282 referring domains on the easiest keywords and 1,571 on the hardest, after the
  report excluded giant platforms like YouTube and Amazon and any domain with fewer than 50 referring domains. Small sites
  weren't measured at all. The ranges are also wide, at 518 to 5,765 for the middle half
  of domains on the hardest keywords, so sites with very different link profiles get cited.
Which page: cited pages often don't rank for the query
Ranking for a query and being cited for it are drifting apart. Ahrefs found 76% of pages cited in AI

articles.title: Not Everything Needs an LLM
articles.content:
Not everything needs an LLM
How we use decision models
Jina Yoon
Nov 09, 2026
50
12
5
Share
LLMs love to yap. Ask a simple question and you get a few hundred words of "it depends." It's annoying as hell.
This is why we love
decision models like Jev
for simpler tasks. You ask a structured question and get a typed answer with a probability, which looks something like this:
Noul.
Are hedgehogs mammals? → Yes, 0.99
Choice.
Which animal family do hedgehogs belong to? → Mammal, 0.99
Score.
What is the current conservation status of hedgehogs? → Least Concern, 0.77
Whereas LLMs return free-form and overly confident prose, decision models make model uncertainty explicit. In a calibrated model, answers that score 0.8 are right about 80% of the time. That means a score of 0.5 is a coin flip.
We've been experimenting with them at PostHog and several use cases have made it to production. This is everything we've learned about using decision models so far: when to use them, how to use them, and mistakes to avoid.
1. Use them to gate expensive LLM calls
Decision models are up to 444.6x cheaper and 193.6x faster than frontier models,
1
so you can use them to check whether you even need to make an expensive LLM call at all.
We do this in a pipeline that scrubs personal info in
Replay Vision
, our product that watches and summarizes user session recordings for you. Here's how it works:
Each session summary goes through 2 yes/no questions from a decision model. Using narrow questions like this cuts false flags to about a tenth of what a single question produced.
1. “Does this name a real person?”
2. “Does this show contact details or an ID?”
If either scores 0.4 or above, Gemini rewrites the summary without the personal info and it gets checked again.
Otherwise, it's clean and passes through the gate.
In production
, 98.7% skip the LLM call entirely.
Without the decision model, we'd have to keep fussing with prompts and regexes that miss things, or sending every summary to Gemini to catch the 1% that need it.
But remember they make mistakes
A probability score of 0.85 still means ~150 wrong answers per 1,000 checks, so plan ahead for false positives and false negatives.
In the PII example, a false positive only costs us an extra LLM call, whereas a false negative stores personal data as clean. That's why we set the threshold low at 0.4.
When false positives are the costlier mistake, use
higher
thresholds. For example, we recently updated the PostHog in Slack bot, so it can answer questions
without being tagged
. To avoid being annoying, it checks every message in a channel to see (1) whether it's asking for information, and (2) whether PostHog could answer it. Only messages that pass both at 0.85+ go through.
Takeaway:
Use decision models to filter jobs before they hit an expensive LLM call, and set the threshold based on which mistake costs you more.
2. Use them as model routers
Our
PostHog in Slack
bot also uses a decision model as a
model router
.
When the bot gets tagged, it first checks whether the message asked for a specific model. If not, one
choice
question picks from the list:
“Pick the cheapest option that will most likely finish the task correctly on the first try. A failed run costs more than a smarter option.”
Each option in the list carries a short note on what that model is good for. GPT Luna is described as “a light and very cheap model. Good for short answers, lookups, summaries and very small edits.” The decision model then scores the request against each option’s text.
But don't assume they're interchangeable
Different tasks, models, and providers all have different thresholds.
We were experimenting with using them to auto-merge similar logs in
Error Tracking
and found that thresholds changed between v1 and v2 of the same model. We had to make its thresholds configurable per PostHog project and keep the judge in shadow mode while recalibrating based on
hand-labeled data
.
This is one of the reasons why
Fernando
on our growth team pushed for a model-agnostic interface early. We now have an internal AI gateway for swapping and testing models, including self-hosted ones.
Takeaway:
Use a
choice
question to route free-form LLM requests to the cheapest model that can handle it. Keep in mind that thresholds don't carry over, so set them per task and per model.
3. Use them for face-value checks
If a question requires more context or chains of reasoning, it's better to use an LLM. However, you can still use a decision model if you have a way to flatten, or pre-process the input, so it's checkable at face-value.
In Replay Vision, when a user searches for a theme like "onboarding friction," there's a chance for the query to return a few unexpected results because of the way embedding distance works.
A decision model can’t "Rank the top 10 sessions that contain summaries that match the user's search query." It’s too complicated.
Instead, we use the embeddings first to derive an initial list of session recordings to pass to the decision model. Then, the only task left for the decision model is to look at how closely each result in the list matches the user's original search term:
"Does this summary describe a session that matches what the search looks for?"
Results are then
reranked
by that probability. On 20 test queries, this improved ranking quality by about 25%.
But avoid multi-step reasoning
We've tried
using a decision model
for multi-step reasoning before. Before embeddings were ready in Replay Vision, we tried ranking a "Highlights" feed of sessions worth a human's time. The questions were:
Is this session worth watching?
If so, why is it worth watching? (With choices like “error on screen,” “slow or stuck,” “user confused”, “user gave up", etc.)
Processing these two questions in order required an hourly job that sent large requests – up to 32 sessions and 12-38k tokens each – which flooded the model server and blocked other products' calls for hours.
So yes, technically, you can chain decision models into multi-step judgments, but it's not operationally worth it. Leave that to LLMs, or do the heavy lifting before the decision model sees the data like in the embedding search example above.
Takeaway:
Decision models judge what's in front of them in a single pass. Leave multi-step reasoning to LLMs.
4. Use them in place of overqualified LLMs
Decision models can take any job where an LLM is overkill, either because it's too slow or too expensive.
One example is our
smarter chart picker
for SQL queries. PostHog used to pick a visualization using deterministic rules like:
A date column, a number column and multiple rows → Line chart
Two or more text columns plus a number → Heatmap
Any number column → Bar chart
Now, a decision model looks at both the SQL itself if your org opts in, and the first three rows of the results to suggest a better chart.
The example below is based on a simple query about pageviews by browser. The original rules picked a basic aggregate line chart; with Jev, it chose a bar chart split by browser:
But keep LLMs for open-ended jobs
Anything more open-ended should still go to an LLM.
Still, out of curiosity, we tried Jev on ranking our internal PR review agent's findings with five noul questions that roughly asked if the change is worth a developer's attention. The results were inconclusive with an AUC of 0.52.
If Jev were an LLM, we’d solve this by sending more context, but Jev can’t handle large requests. Its long-context mode is also slower and less accurate.
2
Typical decision models just aren’t built for this kind of reasoning.
Hybrid decision models like
Jeeves
can help bridge this gap, though. Developed by our
in-house AI research team
, Jeeves is a decision model that reasons before deciding when it’s unsure.
It's now our default for any decision call at PostHog that doesn't name a model, and there are similar variations by other developers, like
Kev
.
Takeaway:
Use decision models as evaluators for inputs that are too simple for a language model, yet too fuzzy for a regex. Anything more complex is still too much to hand over to a decision model. For now, at least.

articles.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
articles.content:
Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage.
For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work.
Content Assessment: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review

A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review."
News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat
Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff
Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found.
In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it.
What the Harvard data measured
How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data.
The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months.
The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI.
The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report.
Drafts went up and finished issues did not
With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start.
Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written.
The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review.
Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue
The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change.
AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity.
That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending.
Employment did not move either
Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally.
Legal AI tools are designed around a similar checkpoint
Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file.
Cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate.
For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings.
The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach.
None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms.
Document review offers a partial precedent

runanywhere.ai
TrnRT
is an open inference engine for large language models on AWS Trainium. It serves an OpenAI-compatible API
from one
trn2.48xlarge
, runs decode as NKI megakernels (about one kernel per layer half), and keeps a prefix cache
across device and host memory.
GLM-5.3-Flash is the first supported model; more open models are on the way.
How we built it, with the AgentX results:
Serving GLM-5.3-Flash on one Trainium2 box with NKI layer megakernels
.
Highlights
Feature
What it does
NKI megakernels
One fused kernel per layer half for decode: KDA attention, the fused DSA layer, mHC and the MoE FFN.
1M-token context
Sparse attention (top 2,048) and linear attention, with fixed-size state.
Prefix cache
A radix tree over FP8 KV pages, plus a host-memory tier for evicted pages and state checkpoints.
Two engines per box
Each engine is tensor-parallel over 32 logical NeuronCores, behind a session-affine router.
OpenAI API
Chat and completions, streaming, tool calls and reasoning output.
Offline compile
Every graph is built on a CPU host; the serving box loads them and compiles nothing by default.
Quickstart
You need Docker, a
trn2.48xlarge
to serve on, and any x86_64 host to compile on. New to Trainium? Start with
docs/AWS.md
.

&&

$(
python3 -c
'
import trnrt; print(trnrt.__version__)
'

\
  --build-arg TRNRT_REVISION=
$(
git rev-parse HEAD
)
-t trnrt
.

(any x86_64 host, no NeuronCore needed; takes hours)

How it works
Decode is not limited by memory bandwidth here; small instructions, kernel boundaries and exposed collectives dominate it. So
each decode megakernel follows three rules: keep the working set in SBUF, use both physical cores symmetrically, and move
the collectives into the kernel.

walks through every kernel.
